lines.say: A lawyer whose firm sold lawsuit settlements that never existed. A businessman recorded by his own employee. A tax-exchange company that spent its clients' money. An offshore bank. And the biggest name of all.

scene.title: Fifty Years|or More
scene.sub: Five Ponzi schemes · five federal sentences

lines.say: Number five. Fifty years.
Scott Rothstein was a lawyer in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. He ran his scheme, the Justice Department said, through his own law firm, Rothstein Rosenfeldt and Adler.

scene.kicker: U.S. ATTORNEY · SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF FLORIDA
scene.title: A billion-dollar Ponzi scheme
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jun 9, 2010

lines.say: The pitch: confidential settlements of civil lawsuits, sold to investors at a discount and repaid over time at full face value. The money, investors were told, would be held in the firm's trust account.

scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jun 9, 2010

lines.say: The Justice Department put it plainly: the purported investment vehicles never existed.

scene.title: “never existed”
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jun 9, 2010

lines.say: To make them look real, prosecutors said, Rothstein and others created false bank documents, false online bank account information, and false settlement agreements and promissory notes.

scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jun 9, 2010

lines.say: Then they went further. Without its clients' knowledge, his firm had settled a lawsuit it filed for them, in the other side's favor. To hide it, prosecutors said, they created a false federal court order, purportedly signed by a U.S. District Judge, saying the clients had won about twenty-three million dollars.
lines.show: Then they went further. Without its clients' knowledge, his firm had settled a lawsuit it filed for them, in the other side's favor. To hide it, prosecutors said, they created a false federal court order, purportedly signed by a U.S. District Judge, saying the clients had won about $23 million.

scene.title: A false federal court order
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jun 9, 2010

lines.say: To collect it, the clients were told to post bonds. They wired about fifty-seven million dollars to a trust account he controlled.
lines.show: To collect it, the clients were told to post bonds. They wired about $57 million to a trust account he controlled.

scene.title: About $57 million
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jun 9, 2010

lines.say: From around two thousand five through November two thousand nine, he and others took in about one point two billion dollars.
lines.show: From around 2005 through November 2009, he and others took in about $1.2 billion.

scene.label: obtained from investors
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, S.D. Fla. — release, Jan 27, 2010

lines.say: He pleaded guilty to five counts, including racketeering conspiracy. On June ninth, two thousand ten, Judge James Cohn sentenced him to fifty years.
lines.show: He pleaded guilty to five counts, including racketeering conspiracy. On June 9, 2010, Judge James Cohn sentenced him to 50 years.

lines.say: He went on to cooperate with prosecutors. But in two thousand eighteen, after prosecutors said he had given them false information, the judge let them withdraw an earlier offer to reduce his sentence. The fifty years stood.
lines.show: He went on to cooperate with prosecutors. But in 2018, after prosecutors said he had given them false information, the judge let them withdraw an earlier offer to reduce his sentence. The 50 years stood.

scene.src: Associated Press, Apr 16, 2018

lines.say: Number four. Also fifty years.
Tom Petters, of Wayzata, Minnesota, bought companies including Fingerhut, Polaroid and Sun Country Airlines. The Justice Department said he paid for them with proceeds of his fraud.

scene.kicker: PETTERS GROUP WORLDWIDE · PER THE JUSTICE DEPARTMENT
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: At the center was Petters Company, Inc. Investors lent it money to buy electronics that would be resold to big-box retailers, like Costco and Sam's Club, at a profit. However, the Justice Department said, no such purchases were made.

scene.title: “entirely fabricated”
scene.src: Criminal complaint & FBI affidavit, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. 08-MJ-364 (Oct 2008) · U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: A Walmart security official told agents that the vendor number on Petters' Sam's Club purchase orders was fictitious.

scene.title: “fictitious”
scene.src: Criminal complaint & FBI affidavit, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. 08-MJ-364 (Oct 2008)

lines.say: From two thousand three to September two thousand eight, about thirty-five billion dollars was wired into one account that only Petters and one employee were authorized to use. None of the deposits came from retailers.
lines.show: From 2003 to September 2008, about $35 billion was wired into one account that only Petters and one employee were authorized to use. None of the deposits came from retailers.

scene.title: About $35 billion
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: The money passed through two so-called vendors. One of them, the Justice Department said, was a sham company with its headquarters above a car wash, a few miles from Petters' headquarters. It did no real business. Money only flowed one way: to Petters' company.

scene.src: U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: The employee who shared that account was Deanna Coleman. On September eighth, two thousand eight, she and her attorney went to the authorities. She agreed to wear a recording device.
lines.show: The employee who shared that account was Deanna Coleman. On September 8, 2008, she and her attorney went to the authorities. She agreed to wear a recording device.

scene.title: September 8, 2008
scene.src: Criminal complaint & FBI affidavit, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. 08-MJ-364 (Oct 2008) · U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: Within the first few hours of her recordings, the Justice Department said, Petters was heard admitting that purchase orders were fake, and claiming divine intervention was the only explanation for how they could have got away with this for so long.
lines.show: Within the first few hours of her recordings, the Justice Department said, Petters was heard admitting that purchase orders were "fake," and claiming "divine intervention" was the only explanation for how they "could of got away with this for so long."

scene.title: “divine intervention”
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: On the recordings, the FBI agent wrote, Petters also talked about fleeing the country. On September twenty-fourth, agents searched his headquarters and his home. On October third, he was arrested.
lines.show: On the recordings, the FBI agent wrote, Petters also talked about fleeing the country. On September 24, agents searched his headquarters and his home. On October 3, he was arrested.

scene.title: Fleeing the country
scene.src: Criminal complaint & FBI affidavit, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. 08-MJ-364 (Oct 2008)

lines.say: Petters went to trial. On December second, two thousand nine, the jury convicted him on all twenty counts. Prosecutors argued for the maximum the counts allowed: three hundred thirty-five years.
lines.show: Petters went to trial. On December 2, 2009, the jury convicted him on all 20 counts. Prosecutors argued for the maximum the counts allowed: 335 years.

scene.title: 335 years
scene.src: Gov't Position Regarding Sentencing, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. No. 08-364, Dkt. 388 · Judgment, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. No. 08-364, Dkt. 400 (Apr 8, 2010)

lines.say: On April eighth, two thousand ten, Judge Richard Kyle gave him six hundred months. Fifty years. The U.S. Attorney's office called it the longest prison term ever ordered in a financial fraud case in Minnesota history.
lines.show: On April 8, 2010, Judge Richard Kyle gave him 600 months. 50 years. The U.S. Attorney's office called it the longest prison term ever ordered in a financial fraud case in Minnesota history.

scene.title: 600 months · 50 years
scene.src: Judgment, U.S. v. Petters, D. Minn. No. 08-364, Dkt. 400 (Apr 8, 2010) · U.S. Attorney, D. Minn. — release, Apr 8, 2010

lines.say: On Petters' own testimony at trial, the judge said: It just didn't pass the smell test.
lines.show: On Petters' own testimony at trial, the judge said: "It just didn't pass the smell test."

scene.q: It just didn't pass the smell test.
scene.doc: JUDGE RICHARD H. KYLE · AT SENTENCING

lines.say: A federal appeals court upheld the conviction and the sentence. The Supreme Court declined to review it.
lines.show: A federal appeals court upheld the conviction and the sentence. The Supreme Court declined to review it.

lines.say: Number three. One hundred years. And the smallest dollar figure on this list.

Edward Okun owned The ten thirty-one Tax Group. The name comes from Section ten thirty-one of the tax code. Sell an investment property, leave the proceeds with a company called a qualified intermediary, buy a new property within a set time, and you can put off the capital gains tax.
lines.show: Edward Okun owned The 1031 Tax Group. The name comes from Section 1031 of the tax code. Sell an investment property, leave the proceeds with a company called a qualified intermediary, buy a new property within a set time, and you can put off the capital gains tax.

scene.kicker: SECTION 1031 · AS THE JUSTICE DEPARTMENT EXPLAINED IT
items: Deposit the proceeds with a qualified intermediary
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, E.D. Va. — release, Nov 17, 2011

lines.say: Clients were promised their money would be used solely for those exchanges. Instead, the evidence at trial showed, Okun and others misappropriated about one hundred twenty-six million dollars of client funds.
lines.show: Clients were promised their money would be used solely for those exchanges. Instead, the evidence at trial showed, Okun and others misappropriated about $126 million of client funds.

scene.kicker: U.S. ATTORNEY · EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
scene.title: About $126 million
scene.src: U.S. Attorney, E.D. Va. — release, Nov 17, 2011

lines.say: It paid for his lavish lifestyle, his companies' expenses and commercial real estate. It also bought more qualified intermediary companies, and with them, more client money to take.

scene.kicker: WHERE THE MONEY WENT · PER THE JUSTICE DEPARTMENT

scene.cite: Memorandum Opinion, U.S. v. Okun, E.D. Va. No. 3:08cr132, Dkt. 324 (Aug 27, 2009)

lines.show: The evidence also showed he had employees withdraw $15,000 in cash and smuggle it to his personal yacht in the Bahamas, to avoid federal currency reporting requirements.

lines.show: On March 19, 2009, a jury in Richmond, Virginia, convicted him of fraud, money laundering, bulk cash smuggling and perjury, among other charges. On August 4, Judge Payne sentenced him to 100 years.

lines.say: Number two. One hundred and ten years.

R. Allen Stanford was chairman of the board of Stanford International Bank, based on the Caribbean island of Antigua. It sold certificates of deposit. By the end of two thousand eight, the SEC said, about eight billion dollars of them.
lines.show: R. Allen Stanford was chairman of the board of Stanford International Bank, based on the Caribbean island of Antigua. It sold certificates of deposit. By the end of 2008, the SEC said, about $8 billion of them.

scene.kicker: STANFORD INTERNATIONAL BANK · PER THE SEC

lines.say: For at least a decade, the SEC alleged, Stanford and his chief financial officer executed a massive Ponzi scheme.

scene.title: “a massive Ponzi scheme”
scene.src: SEC First Amended Complaint, N.D. Tex. 3:09-cv-0298, Feb 27, 2009

lines.say: Where did the money go? According to the government's appeals brief, only about a quarter of the bank's reported assets were invested the way the bank described. Stanford siphoned the remaining seventy-five percent, known as Tier Three, to his companies, real estate purchases, and lifestyle.
lines.show: Where did the money go? According to the government's appeals brief, only about a quarter of the bank's reported assets were invested the way the bank described. Stanford siphoned the remaining 75%, "Tier 3," to his companies, real estate purchases, and lifestyle.

scene.title: “Tier 3” · 75%

lines.say: In March two thousand twelve, a Houston jury convicted him on thirteen of fourteen counts. That June, Judge David Hittner sentenced him to one hundred ten years, for what the Justice Department called a twenty-year investment fraud scheme in which he misappropriated seven billion dollars.
lines.show: In March 2012, a Houston jury convicted him on 13 of 14 counts. That June, Judge David Hittner sentenced him to 110 years, for what the Justice Department called a 20-year investment fraud scheme in which he misappropriated $7 billion.
